messages.content: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

output:
**Opening section — ~260 words**

---

The alert fires at 3:47 a.m. Checkout p99 latency has gone from 240 ms to nine seconds. Your dashboard confirms it, a red line climbing off the top of the panel, and then it stops being useful — because the next question is *which* checkouts, and the dashboard was built by someone who never thought to ask.

That gap is the whole argument.

Monitoring answers questions you wrote down in advance. It's a set of pre-registered guesses about how the system will break: CPU, memory, error rate, the four golden signals. Those guesses are fine. They catch the failures you've already had, and they do nothing for the failure you haven't had yet, which is the one currently costing you money.

Observability is the property of a system that lets you ask a question nobody anticipated and get an answer without shipping new code. Not a vendor, and not the three pillars everyone recites at conferences. A property. Either you have enough detail in the data coming out of production to slice it by customer ID, region, feature flag and deploy SHA at 3:47 a.m., or you don't, and no amount of Grafana will conjure it.

Teams underrate this because the cost lands in the wrong column. Instrumentation looks like overhead during the sprint. It pays out during the incident, when the difference between a fifteen-minute recovery and a four-hour one is whether somebody has to add a log line and wait for a deploy.
